The đàn nhị (chữ Nôm: 彈二) is a two-string bowed instrument of Vietnam, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.322-71, belonging to the Chinese huqin family. One end of the soundbox is usually covered with snakeskin, and it is played with a bow. The forms differ: the one popularly called đàn cò is close to the Chinese erxian, the Khmer tro and the Thai saw duang, while the one called đàn nhị is closer to the modern erhu. It was often played together with the đàn gáo in the past, though this is rarer today; in the 'renovated national music' line-up the traditionally hand-made instrument has mostly been replaced by the Chinese erhu. Some Austroasiatic peoples in Vietnam have similar instruments.

In the past the two names mostly meant the form now called đàn cò; its construction is close to the Chinese erxian, the Khmer tro and the Thai saw duang, and a later đàn nhị closer to the modern Chinese erhu also appeared. Early on it was often played together with the đàn gáo, like the paired use of bowed instruments in Cantonese music and in Thailand; as the đàn gáo declined, this pairing became less common. In the renovated national music ensemble the traditional hand-made instrument has mostly been replaced by the erhu bought from China.

The neck is of hard wood, and the head is finely carved. The strings are high-tension silk or a mixed material. The bow stick is of bamboo or light wood, with horsehair for good friction. The skin may be snakeskin or another natural leather, to strengthen the resonance. Some details use bone or carved wood decoration.

Its range is broad, able to play a high, far-reaching melody or a low, winding phrase. The instrument sounds by the friction of a horsehair bow on silk strings, and the wooden cylindrical soundbox gives a warm, penetrating sound. Compared with the bright clarity of the Chinese erhu, the Vietnamese đàn nhị is quieter and more reserved; compared with the violin, it lacks the sharpness of the Western instrument and holds more poetry and world-weariness. Its tone has soft harmonics, and in traditional Vietnamese folk song it can fully express the emotional tension and cultural meaning of the music, making it an indispensable soul instrument of Southeast Asian traditional music.
